bib.title: The Tasteful Agent: Measuring and Improving Taste in Long-Horizon Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The Tasteful Agent: Measuring and Improving Taste in Long-Horizon Tasks" (Taste-Bench). Wenbo Pan (CityU Hong Kong; work done as a Microsoft intern), Zhichao Liu (independent), Shujie Liu, Jingying Zeng, Chin-Yew Lin, Xianfeng Tang, Yan Lu, Qi He (Microsoft), Xiaohua Jia (CityU HK). arXiv:2609.25804v2 [cs.AI], 23 Sep 2026, header "Preprint September 2026". No peer-reviewed venue. Code: github.com/wbopan/tastebench. Data: huggingface wenbopan/taste-bench.

COVERAGE: All 33 pages, 103,116 chars, read in full (main text, all appendices A-H, the prompts, Tables 1-12). References skimmed. `figures.py captions` printed nothing, so the figure captions below come from the extracted text. Ledger row for 2609.25804 already has pillar eval, note 06-evaluating-agents.md, status downloaded, tier 4.

TARGET NOTE FIT
- Best section: "Outcome and trajectory" in 06-evaluating-agents.md. Add one paragraph after the survey-gap paragraph ("short in diagnosing specific agent failures") and the SayCan plan-vs-execution paragraph. Taste-Bench is a third axis: decision quality at a fork, not path or outcome.
- The note already covers: outcome vs trajectory, progress rate, plan vs execution (SayCan), failure localisation (Terminal-Bench, arXiv 2607.09510), pass@k/pass^k, and judge design for web agents.
- The note lacks: hindsight-labelled decision forks, evaluating a model's choice before the outcome is visible, and "does a judgment aid raise agent success" evidence.
- Secondary fit: the both-orders scoring rule (correct only if right in both orders, so chance is 25%) sharpens 05-llm-as-judge.md line 194 (position bias, "count a win only if it holds both ways"). Add a citation and a references row there too.
- Not a fit for 14/15, which are about judge calibration.

CORE CLAIM
An agent's "taste" is its ability to pick the better direction at a decision fork before the outcome is visible. It can be measured without human annotation. Fork labels come from the recorded outcomes of parallel attempts that diverge, or from detours where an agent abandons one approach and recovers. Frontier models do poorly. Accuracy falls as the deciding evidence moves later in the trajectory, and more reasoning effort does not help. A student distilled from a teacher that sees the answer transfers to unseen tasks and raises a small executor's SWE-bench Pro success.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Best model gets 59.7% on Taste-Bench.
 number: 59.7% Average; GPT-5.5 59.5%; Claude Opus 5 55.5%; random is 25%
 setup: 502 questions (390 engineering, 112 research). 14 models, one shared prompt and 65,536-token budget, no visible chain of thought, a single run per model. "Accuracy" counts a question only if both A/B orders are right. Average is the 1:1 mean of the research and engineering accuracies. Unparseable answers count as wrong. Interval is a 95% item bootstrap.
 quote: "GPT-5.6 Sol is the best model, with an Average accuracy of 59.7%, and GPT-5.5 is close behind at 59.5%"
 where: Sec 4.2, p.5; Fig 3, p.6; Table 4, p.25
2. Accuracy falls with the time horizon of the deciding evidence.
 number: 62.3% (in prefix) to 42.9% (inferable) to 31.5% (next step) to 21.0% (more work)
 setup: mean over the 14 models. Levels are annotated by one judge, GPT-5.5, which is shown the supported label. Level sizes are 158, 219, 56 and 69. "More work" merges two scores (56 + 13 questions).
 quote: "the mean over the 14 models falls from 62.3% at the in-prefix level to 21.0% at the more-work level, near the 25% score of random guessing."
 where: Sec 4.3, p.6-7; Table 6, p.27
3. Extra reasoning effort does not change accuracy.
 number: Sol -0.2 points (95% CI [-3.2, +2.8]); Luna +2.2 points (CI [-1.6, +6.0])
 setup: two models only, three effort settings each (Sol low/xhigh/max; Luna none/high/max), same 502 questions, 6,024 responses. Logistic budget x horizon interaction p = 0.80 (Sol) and 0.82 (Luna).
 quote: "moving from the lowest to the highest reasoning-effort setting changes the accuracy of GPT-5.6 Sol by −0.2 points and that of GPT-5.6 Luna by +2.2 points."
 where: Sec 4.4, p.7; App D.4, p.26-27
4. Distillation transfers to unseen tasks.
 number: student 47.9% vs base 30.0% (+17.9 points). Training fold, single order: 48.6% to 92.9%.
 setup: base Qwen3.6-27B with LoRA (rank 16). Teacher is the same model shown the supported candidate. Loss is a forward KL on teacher-sampled reasoning plus a calibration pass. Trained on the 390 engineering questions in two task-disjoint folds, each evaluated on the other fold. Pooled out-of-fold, both-orders scoring. The student answers both orders correctly on 187 of 390 questions, the base on 117.
 quote: "the student reaches an accuracy of 47.9% and the base model 30.0%"
 where: Sec 5.2, p.9; App G.3, p.30-31
5. Student advice raises end-to-end SWE-bench Pro success.
 number: no advice 14.6%; correct advice 39.0% (+24.4 points, McNemar p ≤ 0.004); student advice 33.7% (+19.1 points)
 setup: 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks with 98 forks. Executor is SWE-agent 1.1.0 with Qwen3.6-27B, thinking off, 75 model calls. Advice is a note per fork ("known trap" / "route that avoided the trap") put in the first user message. The student picks the supported candidate on 77 of 98 forks.
 quote: "the executor reaches a success rate of 33.7% with student advice, a gain of 19.1 percentage points over no advice."
 where: Sec 5.3, p.9; App H, p.31-33
6. Taste is only partly predicted by SWE-bench Verified.
 number: r = +0.63 (R² = 0.39) on the Average; r = +0.37 on the engineering subset. The top four on Verified are within 4.0 points there but 10.7 points apart on Taste-Bench.
 setup: 11 models (3 dropped for more than 9% unparsable). Verified scores come from the Vals AI leaderboard. The 95% CI on r is [+0.04, +0.89] for the Average and [−0.30, +0.79] for engineering.
 quote: "the Pearson correlation between the Average and SWE-bench Verified is r = +0.63, so SWE-bench Verified explains R2 = 0.39 of the variance between the models."
 where: Sec 4.5, p.7; App D.2, p.25
7. Detour forks are harder than parallel forks, more than domain matters.
 number: means over 14 models are 58.1% (parallel engineering), 50.9% (parallel research), 50.8% (detour research), 35.9% (detour engineering)
 quote: "the mean over the 14 models is 58.1% on parallel engineering, 50.9% on parallel research, 50.8% on detour research, and 35.9% on detour engineering."
 where: App D.1, p.25
8. Label quality check.
 number: 98.8% agreement (170 of 172 explicit A/B judgments), κ = 0.973 between reviewers
 setup: 100 sampled questions (70 released, 15 removed as trivial, 15 removed as non-unanimous). Two reviewers. The agreement stage comes AFTER they see the recorded continuations and outcomes. They agree on 73 of 74 questions where both chose A or B.
 quote: "Of the 172 explicit A/B judgments, 170 agree with the mined label, yielding 98.8% agreement"
 where: Sec 3.3, p.5; App F, p.28
9. Construction yield.
 number: 4,657 candidate forks, 1,809 pass the generator rubric, 729 survive the trivial filter, 502 released (10.8%)
 setup: engineering pool is 2,677 graded rollouts by GPT-5.4/5.5 agents on 517 SWE-bench Pro tasks. Research pool is 1,132 METR MALT runs on 47 RE-Bench/HCAST tasks (older Claude and DeepSeek V3 agents). The generator is GPT-5.6 Sol. The judge panel is Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, Llama 4 Maverick and Mistral Large 3.
 quote: "The generator proposes 4,657 candidate forks from the two pools, and 10.8% of them pass all filters."
 where: Sec 3.3, p.4; Fig 8, p.20
10. The models spend the most reasoning tokens where they are least accurate.
 number: lowest accuracy at "more work", between 13.0% and 23.2% over the six reasoning conditions
 quote: "the two models produce the most reasoning tokens at the more-work level, which is also the level with the lowest accuracy"
 where: Sec 4.4, p.7; App D.4, p.27

LIMITS
Stated by the authors:
- SWE-bench Verified scores are public numbers from one harness, and the reasoning-effort setting is not matched across models.
- The correlation interval is wide.
- Only 13 questions get the top time-horizon score, so it was merged.
- Dual-use risk is acknowledged.

Unstated (my reading):
- No human taste baseline. Reviewers' pre-disclosure choices were collected (App F.1) but never reported. The 98.8% only shows the label is consistent with the outcome once the outcome is shown. It does not show the outcome was caused by the decision.
- Labels rest on one pass and one fail per pair, with no repeats. The rubric rejects crashes, typos and luck by generator judgment.
- Some labels look like hidden-test spec-guessing. Example: the Element Web question (App B) is decided by a hidden deep-equality test.
- Selection effects:
  - Questions are kept only if at least one of four judges fails them without the trajectory (Llama 4 Maverick gets 34.7% on released items), and all four must confirm the label with the full record. Difficulty is partly built in, and subtle-hindsight forks are filtered out.
  - The time-horizon labeller (GPT-5.5) is also a tested model and sees the answer.
  - The generator (GPT-5.6 Sol) is also the top model.
  - GPT-5.4/5.5 agents produced the engineering trajectories, so family self-preference is possible and not examined.
  - The horizon is confounded with cell: parallel research holds 21 of the 69 "more work" items. "Requires predicting later work" is a causal reading of a correlation.
- Small and clustered: the research half has 112 questions from only 8 (parallel) and 22 (detour) tasks. The item bootstrap ignores task clustering.
- The reasoning-budget test covers only two models. The Luna CI reaches +6.0, and Luna's research accuracy rises 43.8% to 54.5% with effort (App D.4), so "does not improve" is weaker than the headline.
- End-to-end:
  - The advice was written from forks mined from earlier runs of the very same tasks. It carries "known trap" text and a mandatory-verification contract (App H). There is no control for advice with just the verification contract, and no significance test for student advice vs no advice.
  - In deployment such forks would not be available in advance.
  - 21 of 98 student forks pointed to the wrong route, and the paper does not analyse the harm.
- Dated: model names (GPT-5.6, Claude Opus 5, etc.) and the Verified scores will shift.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- 33.7% cannot be k/41 for a single run (13/41 = 31.7%, 14/41 = 34.1%), while 14.6% = 6/41 and 39.0% = 16/41 can. The number of executor runs is not stated.
- Sol xhigh in Table 7 gets 55.6% over all questions and 78.5% in-prefix. The main run gives 292/502 = 58.2% pooled and 79.7% in-prefix (Table 6). The same model and setting differ by about 2.6 points between runs. That is as large as the effect the reasoning test is trying to detect. The paper gives no run-to-run variance.
- Grok 4.20 scores 15.7% (below chance) with 459 of 1,004 unparsable. GPT-5.4 Mini has 112 and Nano has 93 unparsable. These parse failures depress Figure 3 rankings for those models, yet they are excluded only from the SWE-bench correlation.
- Sec 4.4 and Finding 3 say budget "does not improve" accuracy, but Luna's research subset rises 43.8% to 54.5%.
- Student advice picks the supported candidate on 287/390 questions, higher than its 187/390 both-orders accuracy, because the advice rule combines both orders' log-odds. The advice numbers are therefore not the headline accuracy.
- Table 2 "Proposed" sums to 1,809 (rubric-passing), not the 4,657 that the text calls "proposed".

BUILDS ON
- SWE-bench / SWE-bench Pro (Jimenez 2024; Deng 2026)
- RE-Bench (Wijk 2025), HCAST (Rein 2025), MALT (Parikh & Wijk 2025)
- Position-bias work (Shi et al. 2025)
- SDPO self-distillation (Hübotter 2026), context distillation (Askell 2021; Snell 2022), STaR, LEAP, on-policy distillation (Agarwal 2024), LoRA (Hu 2022)
- Process supervision (Lightman 2024; Math-Shepherd), Agent-as-a-Judge, AgentRewardBench
- Failure attribution (Who&When; AgenTracer)
- Research-outcome prediction (Wen 2025; Zheng 2026; Baig 2026 "TASTE" proposals; Si 2026 ideation-execution gap)
- Advisor models (Asawa 2026)
- METR time horizon (Kwa 2025)

CODE (verbatim, App A.3, p.18-19, the mechanical ordering check in the detour generator prompt)
"breakpoint_step <= bad_action.step <= wall.step < recovery_action.step <= success[*].step."
Eval prompt (App C, p.24): "Which option is the better technical decision? Return exactly one line: ANSWER: X"
Scoring rule (Sec 3.4): a question is correct only when both the seeded and the reversed order are right. Chance = 25%, an always-first model = 0%.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): ML fork, train a masked LM. Option A reduces model size and trains more steps (final loss 6.56). Option B keeps size and trains fewer steps (7.66). Clearest one-glance picture of a fork.
- Fig 2 (p.4): construction and filtering pipeline.
- Fig 3 (p.6): per-model bars, both-orders solid vs two-order-mean dotted, 95% CIs. The gap shows position bias.
- Fig 4 (p.6): accuracy by time horizon (left) and reasoning budget (right). Best figure candidate for note 06. The falling line from 62.3 to 21.0 and the flat budget curves explain the two main findings.
- Fig 5 (p.7): Taste-Bench vs SWE-bench Verified scatter.
- Fig 6 (p.9): distillation and advice injection diagram.
- Fig 7 (p.9): student 47.9 vs base 30.0 vs Sol 56.9; SWE-bench Pro 14.6 / 33.7 / 39.0.
- Fig 8 (p.20): filtering funnel per cell.

PROBLEMS
- The pypdf extraction is clean, apart from some ligature spacing ("thetasteof") and merged duplicate labels in the figure text (Figs 3-5). No embedded instructions found in the PDF. Prompts inside it are the paper's own benchmark prompts.
- `figures.py captions` returned no output, so captions come from the text.
- Full text saved at /tmp/tp/t.txt (my scratch copy). PDF: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/pan-2026-tasteful-agent.pdf
- Calibration for the editor: the ledger flags this as "narrow and early" (relevance 2, tier 4, 1 citation). The numbers worth keeping are claims 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8, each with its limit.
